requirements.requirement: Create the opsbot identities and provision node1-generated SSH key material needed for access on both nodes.
requirements.summary: opsbot was created with a locked password on both nodes. Node1 generated an Ed25519 key, and the same key fingerprint was present in the authorized-key state on both systems.

requirements.requirement: Allow opsbot on node1 to run commands remotely as opsbot on node2 using SSH keys.
requirements.summary: Direct SSH tests from node1 executed commands on node2 as uid 1001 (opsbot), both before and after the node restarts.

requirements.requirement: Require key-based authentication for opsbot on both systems.
requirements.summary: Effective per-user sshd policy on both nodes enables public keys, disables password and keyboard-interactive authentication, and requires AuthenticationMethods publickey. A password-only attempt against node2 was directly rejected before and after restart.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied. The provider-wide restart protocol was also completed coherently for both nodes: each had a healthy pre-restart state, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered sshd/account/key policy, and restored cross-node command execution. Fixed lifecycle boot identities independently agree with the executor observations.
limitations: Node1's key-only restriction was confirmed through effective sshd configuration and locked-password state, but no direct SSH password-rejection test targeting node1 was captured.
Package-health collection timed out both before and after execution on both nodes, so package consistency could not be independently assessed.

operational_hygiene.summary: Final hygiene was healthy: neither node had failed services, listening endpoints remained equivalent to baseline, and observed temporary-file changes were normal reboot-related systemd directories. The only unnecessary mutations identified were unsupported ChallengeResponseAuthentication directives appended inside Match blocks on node1 and node2. They temporarily made the saved sshd configuration invalid, but validation prevented reload and the directives were promptly removed; no invalid configuration remained. The rest of those commands contributed directly to the final account, key, and SSH-policy state.
